opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that interpretability on its own is fundamentally a diagnostic tool. It lets you look inside a model and say, "Here's a feature that represents deception," or "Here's a circuit that seems to be doing something we don't like." And that's incredibly valuable. But knowing what's wrong with a system isn't the same as being able to fix it. A doctor who can read an MRI perfectly but can't operate is only getting you halfway there.

What we've seen over the last couple of years is that the field has gotten really good at the reading part. Sparse autoencoders, transcoders, attribution graphs: we can now decompose these models into units that humans can actually reason about. But the dominant way we still shape model behavior is post-training: RLHF, fine-tuning, constitutional methods. Those operate at the level of inputs and outputs. They're behavioral. You reward the model for saying the right thing, and you hope the internal changes that produces are the ones you wanted. Often they're not. You get superficial patches, you get the model learning to hide the behavior rather than not having it, you get weird side effects elsewhere.

So the idea behind refactoring is: what if you could close the loop? Use the interpretable decomposition not just to observe the model, but as the actual substrate you edit. If you can identify the mechanisms responsible for an undesirable behavior, you should in principle be able to surgically change or remove those mechanisms, and then verify, using the same interpretability tools, that the change did what you intended and didn't break anything else.

That's why I think of it as the crucial bridge. Alignment ultimately requires that we can *intervene* with confidence, not just *observe*. And the thing that makes refactoring exciting to me is that it turns interpretability from a science into an engineering discipline. In software, refactoring means restructuring code without changing what it's supposed to do, while making it cleaner and easier to reason about. The analogy for models is: can we take this opaque, tangled network and restructure it into something whose behavior we understand and can modify deliberately?

Now, I want to be honest that we're early. The decompositions aren't perfect: there's reconstruction error, features don't always mean exactly what we think, and editing one thing can have ripple effects. But I'd much rather work on making that pipeline more reliable than keep relying purely on behavioral training and hoping the internals come out right. If we're going to trust these systems with increasingly important decisions, we need to be able to say not just "it behaves well on our evals," but "we know why it behaves well, and we put that there on purpose."

r001.rationale: It compares model refactoring to software refactoring and calls the network tangled, but does not clearly liken neural models to legacy codebases with tangled component interactions.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes decomposing a model into interpretable units from using those units as a substrate to edit and deliberately restructure the model.

r003.rationale: It discusses identifying and editing mechanisms, but does not characterize steering as causal evidence that a mechanism contributes to behavior.

r004.rationale: It does not describe steering or generating counterfactual behavior.

r005.rationale: It frames the bridge as intervening in and improving an existing model, but does not say that understanding it determines how to produce desired behavior from the outset.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that interpretability, as it's mostly practiced today, is a reading exercise. You train a model, it's a big opaque blob, and then you go in afterwards with probes, sparse autoencoders, attribution graphs, whatever your tool of choice is, and you try to reconstruct a story about what it's doing. And that work is genuinely valuable. But there's a gap between understanding a system and being able to change it in a way you trust, and I think that gap is where alignment actually lives.

Refactoring is the step that closes that gap. In software, when you refactor, you take code that works but is tangled and you rewrite it so the structure matches the intent, without changing the behavior. You end up with something a human can read, modify, and verify. I think we need the analogous move for models. Once you've identified a feature or a circuit, the question becomes: can I pull that out, give it a clean, legible form, and put it back such that the model still performs the same? If the answer is yes, you've done something much stronger than interpretation. You've demonstrated that your understanding is complete enough to be load-bearing.

And that's the key property for alignment. A lot of alignment failures come down to the fact that we can't say what the model is actually optimizing for, or we can't intervene precisely when we see a problem. If the only tool you have is more training, every fix is a blunt instrument. You patch one behavior and something else shifts that you didn't anticipate. But if you've refactored the parts you care about into components you can read and edit, then alignment starts looking like engineering rather than persuasion. You can audit the thing. You can make a targeted change and verify it held.

The other reason I think it's crucial is that it keeps you honest. It's very easy to produce interpretability results that look compelling and are subtly wrong, because there's no forcing function. Refactoring provides one. If you swap in your clean version and the model's behavior degrades, your story was incomplete. That feedback loop is what turns interpretability from a descriptive science into something you can build on.

So I don't see it as a separate project. I see it as the test of whether interpretability is real, and the mechanism by which it actually becomes useful for making models safe.

r001.rationale: The response compares refactoring models to refactoring software, but it does not liken neural models to legacy codebases with tangled interactions among components.

r002.rationale: It describes extracting a feature or circuit into a legible form and putting it back, but does not distinguish factoring components for understanding from refactoring them into a better implementation.

r003.rationale: The response presents refactoring as a test of whether understanding is complete, but does not identify steering as a causal demonstration that a mechanism contributes to behavior.

r004.rationale: It does not characterize steering as generating counterfactual model behavior.

r005.rationale: It discusses using understanding to make targeted changes to an existing model, but does not frame the bridge as using that understanding to produce models that behave as desired from the outset.

astra-6.text:
Because understanding what a model is doing and being able to change what it’s doing are two different things. Interpretability can give us a description of an internal mechanism. But for alignment, we need to turn that understanding into reliable control over the model’s behavior.

The analogy to software refactoring is useful here. You take something that works but is difficult to reason about, and reorganize it into components with clearer responsibilities. With models, the aspiration is to identify meaningful internal computations and make them more separable, so we can inspect, test, and modify them without unpredictably disrupting everything else.

That also gives us a stronger test of our interpretations. If we think a particular mechanism causes a behavior, can we change that mechanism and get the change we predicted? Can we preserve the capabilities we want while changing the behavior we don’t want?

That wouldn’t solve alignment by itself. We’d still need to decide what behavior we want and establish that our interventions generalize. But it would turn interpretability from a way of observing models into an engineering discipline for changing them. That’s the bridge I think matters.

r001.rationale: It uses a software-refactoring analogy, but does not liken neural models to legacy codebases with tangled component interactions.

r002.rationale: It describes making internal computations separable and changing behavior, but does not clearly distinguish factoring a model into understandable components from refactoring those components into a better implementation.

r003.rationale: It proposes changing an identified mechanism and checking whether the predicted behavioral change follows, presenting intervention as a causal test.

r004.rationale: It discusses changing behavior, but does not characterize steering as generating counterfactual model behavior.

r005.rationale: It frames the bridge as using interpretability to change existing models; it does not say this understanding determines how to produce desired behavior in models from the outset.

sol-6.1.text:
Because understanding what a model is doing doesn’t, by itself, give you control over it. You might identify a feature or a circuit associated with some behavior, but there’s still a gap between saying, “Here’s what we think is happening,” and being able to reliably change it.

Refactoring is a way to close that gap. In software, you refactor to make the structure clearer while preserving the behavior you want. The analogous ambition for models is to take these opaque, distributed computations and reorganize them into components we can understand, test, and modify.

That matters for alignment because we need to be able to make targeted changes without breaking everything else. Can we change a particular behavior, preserve the model’s useful capabilities, and verify that the change holds across different contexts? If we can do that, interpretability becomes more than an observational science—it becomes a basis for engineering.

I wouldn’t say refactoring automatically solves alignment. You still need to specify what you want and establish that your interventions work. But it gives you a path from understanding a system to deliberately shaping it, and that’s the crucial step.

r001.rationale: It compares model refactoring to software refactoring and describes model computations as opaque and distributed, but does not liken neural models to legacy codebases with tangled component interactions.

r002.rationale: It describes reorganizing opaque computations into understandable components, but does not distinguish that factoring step from refactoring those components into a better implementation.

r003.rationale: It discusses targeted changes, but does not identify steering as a causal demonstration that a particular mechanism contributes to behavior.

r004.rationale: It says interventions can change behavior, but does not characterize steering as generating counterfactual model behavior.

r005.rationale: It frames interpretability as a basis for deliberately shaping a system, but does not describe using an existing model’s mechanisms to determine how to produce desired behavior from the outset.
